body: The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit on November 6, 2026, affirmed the dismissal of a suit by AB Realty, LLC, owner of the Yale Park Apartment Complex in Omaha, Nebraska, over the city's 2018 closure of the property. Judge Jonathan A. Kobes wrote for a panel that included Chief Judge Colloton and Judge Gruender.

According to the facts alleged in the complaint and its exhibits, two housing advocates began talking with Yale Park tenants in the summer of 2018, documented conditions and passed complaints to the city, which began planning the closure. Chief Housing Inspector Scott Lane obtained an inspection warrant relying mostly on their information. His application cited suspected health and safety violations in 84 of the complex's 100 units, and the court noted it contained factual errors, including a false statement that an individual plaintiff had refused Lane's request to enter. The city executed the warrant on September 20, 2018, tenants were relocated, and the city ordered that Yale Park could not reopen until the violations were cured. The city later sent notices of about 2,000 violations and prosecuted an individual plaintiff for misdemeanor code violations; a jury convicted on a few counts and acquitted on most.

AB Realty and two individuals filed suit in federal court in March 2019 under 42 U.S.C. Section 1983, according to the CourtListener docket, and AB Realty reopened the complex in the spring of 2021 after repairs. The district court dismissed part of the case, stayed the rest until the criminal case ended, and then dismissed the remaining claims.

On appeal, AB Realty argued the warrant was invalid under Franks v. Delaware because the application falsely said entry had been refused and that police had been called, that inspections had occurred, that threats were made against tenants and that a gas leak caused an explosion. The panel held that even excluding the disputed information, the application established probable cause under the standard for administrative warrants, citing complaints about 84 of 100 units, holes in the roof, untreated natural gas leaks and an admission that maintenance requests had been handled in a "lackadaisical" way. A Nebraska statute requiring a refusal of consent before an inspection warrant issues did not help, the court said, because a violation of state law alone does not state a Section 1983 claim. The due-process claims failed because the complaint did not identify which protected interests were at stake or who violated them. On takings, the court found no per se taking because AB Realty still owns the property, and no regulatory taking because the plaintiffs did not argue one under the Penn Central test.

timeline.label: Housing advocates document conditions at Yale Park and send complaints to the city
City executes an inspection warrant and closes the complex
AB Realty appeals to the city's Property Management Appeals Board
AB Realty and two individuals file suit in federal court
AB Realty reopens Yale Park after repairs
Eighth Circuit affirms dismissal of all claims
